cards.explanation: The reason David gives is that no one alive is righteous before God. David, king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), doesn't hand God a resume. He says, “…for no one alive is righteous before You.” That covers every living person, friends, and he doesn't leave himself out. I think it takes a big heart to walk into a prayer with no bragging at all.

The answer is in darkness. David says the enemy is making him dwell “…in darkness like those long since dead.” That's a heavy line, and I think it hurts to read. I know a little about dark places, friends. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and nobody was going to hand me a flashlight. David puts it plainly in front of God, and that's a good place to put it.

The word is faint. David says, “My spirit grows faint within me…” That's a spirit running low, like a mixer winding down with the batter still in the bowl. He doesn't hide it, either. He says out loud that his heart is dismayed.

David thinks about the work of God's hands. He says, “I consider the work of Your hands.” He also says he remembers the days of old and meditates on all God's works. When he's low, he looks back at what God has done. Good habit, friends. It's like rereading the best batch notes when the oven's acting up.

The answer is False. David says, “I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land.” It's dry ground waiting on rain, not a well-watered garden. That's what I call an honest prayer, friends.

David says he'll be like those who descend to the Pit. He asks, “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” He's saying how much he needs God to answer. The Pit is a picture of the grave, and that's the comparison he reaches for. I think this one is heavy, friends.

The answer is True. David says, “Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.” He's asking for directions, not just rescue. Smart man. I've never once regretted asking for directions, friends, even with a mustache for a pointer.

David flees to God for refuge. He says, “I flee to You for refuge.” He's talking to the LORD, and that's where he runs. The enemy has pursued his soul, and he runs straight to God. That's a smart place to run, friends.

The answer is True. David prays, “May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.” He's asking God's good Spirit to lead him. Level ground sounds good to me, friends. Like a countertop that doesn't wobble when I stamp.

David asks for the sake of God's name. He prays, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” The reason he gives is God's name. I think that's a big deal, friends, since it points his prayer at God and not at himself.

The words are cut off. David prays, “And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies.” He's asking God to do it, and he asks it in God's loving devotion. This is a heavy line, friends. He ends by saying, “…for I am Your servant.”
